Save embeddings to a file, and read them back

Source: R/onnx.R
saveEmbeddings.Rd

Embedding images needs a vision model, and so Python; using embeddings does not. saveEmbeddings() writes what embedImages() or embedTexts() returned to one small file, and loadEmbeddings() reads it back as it was, row names and tiling included, on a computer with no Python at all. Everything dimoose does after embedding (discoverSniglets(), snigletScores(), keyFromSniglets(), keyFromClusters(), featureScores(), ...) works from the loaded embeddings.

Usage

saveEmbeddings(x, file, precision = c("float32", "float16"), model = NULL)

loadEmbeddings(file)

Arguments

x

A numeric matrix or array, or a list of them such as embedImages() returns (entries that are NULL are left out).

file

File to write or read; .safetensors is the usual ending.

precision

"float32", or "float16" for a file half the size. Embeddings have unit length, so 16-bit floats change cosine similarities only in the fourth decimal place.

model

Optional visionModel() the embeddings were made with; its details are stored in the file. Embeddings from loadEmbeddings() keep the model they were loaded with when saved again.

Value

saveEmbeddings() returns file, invisibly. loadEmbeddings() returns what was saved: a matrix or array, or a list of them. If the file records a model, its details are in the result's model attribute.

File format

The file is in the safetensors format, which Python (safetensors.numpy.load_file()), JavaScript and other languages read too:

  • 8 bytes: the length N of the header in bytes, an unsigned 64-bit little-endian integer;

  • N bytes: the header, one JSON object in UTF-8, padded with spaces so that N is a multiple of 8. It has one entry per array, in the order the arrays are stored, named image and patches (for embedImages()), embeddings (for a single matrix) or by the names of the list given. Each entry has dtype ("F32" or "F16"), shape (the dimensions, e.g. [36, 512]) and data_offsets ([begin, end]: the array's first byte and the byte after its last, counted from the end of the header);

  • the arrays' numbers, one array after another with nothing between them, in row-major (C) order: an images x d matrix is stored image by image, an images x tiles x d array image by image and tile by tile.

Numbers are IEEE 754 floats of 4 bytes ("F32") or 2 bytes ("F16"), and always little-endian, whatever the computer that writes or reads the file.

The header's __metadata__ entry is an object of strings: format ("dimoose-embeddings"), version ("1"), single ("true" when x was one array and not a list, so that it is read back as one), rownames.<array> (a JSON array of the row names: image ids or texts; other dimensions' names are not kept), tiles.<array> and empty.<array> (the tiling and the rule for empty tiles, see embedImages(), as numbers separated by commas) and model (a JSON object with the model's details, if there is a model).

loadEmbeddings() also reads safetensors files written by other programs, as long as their arrays are 16-, 32- or 64-bit floats.

Precision

R keeps numbers as 64-bit floats and the file holds 32-bit ones (about 7 significant digits). Vision models compute in 32 bits, so what embedImages() and embedTexts() return is saved and read back exactly; other numbers come back rounded to the nearest 32-bit float. With precision = "float16" every number is rounded to about 3 significant digits: unit-length embeddings change by at most 0.0005 per coordinate. Numbers too large for the chosen precision become Inf, and NA is read back as NaN.

Embeddings that come with dimoose

The embeddings of the package's example photos are in its extdata/embeddings folder, so the examples can be followed with no Python: pics-clip-vit-b-32.safetensors (the 36 fruit photos in extdata/pics, whole photos and 4 x 4 tiles), new-photos-clip-vit-b-32.safetensors (the 6 photos in extdata/new-photos), texts-clip-vit-b-32.safetensors (the prompts of the vision vignette) and montana-bioclip.safetensors (the tree photos in extdata/montana and the names of montanaKey()'s species, embedded with BioCLIP). The folder's README.md says how each was made.

Examples

# stand-ins for embedImages(model, images): 3 images, 2 tiles each, 4 dimensions
emb <- list(image = matrix(rnorm(12), 3, 4, dimnames = list(c("a", "b", "c"), NULL)),
            patches = array(rnorm(24), c(3, 2, 4), dimnames = list(c("a", "b", "c"), NULL, NULL)))
attr(emb$patches, "tiles") <- 1L
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".safetensors")
saveEmbeddings(emb, file)
back <- loadEmbeddings(file)
all.equal(back$image, emb$image, tolerance = 1e-6)
#> [1] TRUE
rownames(back$image)
#> [1] "a" "b" "c"
attr(back$patches, "tiles")
#> [1] 1

# the example photos' embeddings, made with CLIP ViT-B/32: a key with no Python
pics <- loadEmbeddings(system.file("extdata", "embeddings", "pics-clip-vit-b-32.safetensors",
                                   package = "dimoose"))
dim(pics$patches)
#> [1]  36  16 512
attr(pics, "model")$arch
#> [1] "ViT-B-32"
images <- imageSet(system.file("extdata", "pics", package = "dimoose"))
sniglets <- discoverSniglets(pics$patches, k = 40)
scores <- snigletScores(pics$patches, sniglets$centroids)
keyFromSniglets(scores, images, sniglets, method = "rpart")
#> <dimoose key> Key generated from sniglets
#>   5 couplets, 10 leads, 6 taxa, up to 4 steps deep (2.8 on average)
